n=109: JSON dataset in the message. c1 imperative create complement n1 (a doughnut chart); c2 nonfinite called complement n2 (Sales); n3 "7" tied r4 n2→n3; r1 "for" n2→k1 (Jan, Feb); r2 "with" n1→n6 (datasets); n7 = "label North data" (deps label, North, head data); n8 7; n9 9; n10 "label"; n11 South; n12 data; n13 8; n14 10; r3 n1→c2; r5 n6→n7; r6 n7→n8; r7 n7→n10; r8 n8→n9; r9 n10→n11; r10 n10→n12; r11 n12→n13; r12 n13→n14.

JSON structure: [{"label": "North", "data": [7,9]}, {"label": "South", "data": [8,10]}]. The circuit: n7 "label North data" merges label and data into one nominal with head "data"?? Hmm, "label", "North", "data" as deps with head "data". Merging "label North" and "data" into one nominal — the pairing label↔North works (r7 n7→n10 = label→South, hmm).

Chain: n7 (label North data) → n8 (7) → n9 (9); n7 → n10 (label) → n11 (South), n10→n12 (data) → n13 (8) → n14 (10).

Messy but all tokens present, chained in order. The JSON keys/values are held as nominals and tied in order. Plausible-garbled handling. Honestly, a next layer can read the sequence. I'd accept L8? Hmm.

The one nominal n7 = "label North data" with head "data" merges three words from different JSON slots. Would this be "two nominals merged" L3? "label" and "North" are separate JSON tokens; "data" is a key. Hmm.

I'd accept — the content is a data blob; the circuit keeps order and ties. Accept L8.

n=110: "while you're there, I want the marker interval 3 on the revenue trend and I'd like the series name Trajectory on the revenue trend"
c1 declarative "'re" modifier there subject you; c2 declarative want subject I complement n3 (the marker interval); n4 "3" tied r4 n3→n4; r2 "on" n3→n5 (revenue trend); k1 coordination "and" c2, c3; c3 declarative 'd like subject I complement n7 (the series name); n8 Trajectory tied r5 n7→n8; r3 "on" c3→n9.

Good. Accept L8.

n=111: "change the backdrop to a garden full of roses"
c1 imperative change complement n1; r1 "to" c1→n2 ("a garden full": deps a, full, head garden); r2 "of" n2→n3 (roses).

"full" as dependent of "garden" — fine. Accept L8.

n=112: "half the stand-up was grumbling that the numbers were impossible to read from the corridor screen; to settle it, I'd like the numbers back on the right on the sales chart — while you're at it, how about top numbers in tens? going forward, also make the font a bit bigger"
c5 = "I'd like the numbers back on the right on the sales chart" written as **interrogative** with auxiliary 'd, modifier back, subject I, complement the numbers! That's a declarative statement written as interrogative → L1 (the reverse: a declarative written as interrogative).

Yes: "I'd like the numbers back on the right on the sales chart" is not a question. The circuit form=interrogative → L1.

Also c7 fragment modifier "how" with ellipsis=$c5 — ellipsis claiming it shares "like"? "how about top numbers in tens?" — hmm.

Grade L1, quote "I'd like the numbers back on the right".

n=113: "No, make the avatar shaven after all, because the beard still shows."
c1 imperative discourse No, verb make, modifier shaven, modifier after, modifier all, complement n1; r1 "because" c1→c2; c2 declarative still shows subject n2.

"after all" as two modifiers — fine (fixed phrase; as separate modifier words also fine). Accept L8.

n=114: "mirror the boat top to bottom but not left to right, so the bow still points at the harbour"
c1 imperative mirror complements n1 (the boat), n2 (top); r1 "to" n2→n3 (bottom); k1 coordination "but" c1, c2; c2 fragment modifier "not", modifier "left", ellipsis=c1; r2 "to" c2→n4 (right); r3 "so" c1→c3; c3 declarative points subject the bow; r4 "at" c3→n6.

Hmm: "not left to right" — c2 fragment with modifiers "not" and "left", ellipsis c1. Reasonable.

Accept L8.

n=115: "for the monthly ops review on Friday I need the revenue trend legible from the back of the conference room, so make the reference line dashed, grey and horizontal before we circulate it wider and then make the font a bit bigger"
c1 declarative need modifier legible subject I complement the revenue trend; r1 "for" c1→n1; r2 "on" n1→n2; r3 "from" c1→n5; r4 "of" n5→n6; c2 imperative make modifiers dashed, grey, discourse "and", modifier horizontal, complement the reference line; k1 coordination with conjunctions so, and: conjuncts c1, c2, c4; r5 "before" c2→c3 (circulate); c3 declarative circulate modifier wider subject we complement it; c4 imperative then make modifier bigger complements the font, a bit.

Here c1 is declarative — correct (the n=67 counterpart had interrogative). Good.

"discourse and" — the "and" between "grey" and "horizontal" (two modifiers) → discourse allowed per case. Good.

Accept L8.

n=116: "one pie chart, the wedges rides 30%, repairs 25%, spares 45%"
c1 declarative verb "rides" subject n2 (the wedges) complement n3 ("30%"); c2 declarative verb "repairs" complement n4 ("25%"); c3 declarative verb "spares" complement n5 ("45%"); c4 fragment complement n1 (one pie chart); k1 coordination c4, c1, c2, c3.

"repairs" and "spares" held as verbs of declarative clauses — they're labels (nouns) in a list: wedges 30%, repairs 25%, spares 45%. The circuit makes "repairs" and "spares" verbs of declarative clauses → "Its `verb` is a word that is no verb here" → L1? Hmm. "repairs" can be a verb ("he repairs") and a noun. Grammar allows both in isolation. But the message: "one pie chart, the wedges rides 30%, repairs 25%, spares 45%" — a list of label/value pairs. Reading "repairs 25%" as "repairs [conj] 25%" — the verb reading yields "repairs 25%" with no subject. Hmm, "25%" can't be an object of "repairs" sensibly... but grammar-wise "repairs 25%" is a verb + complement.

C1: "the wedges rides 30%" — subject "the wedges", verb "rides". Hmm, that's how "the wedges rides 30%" reads literally... Actually the intended: the wedges ride 30% (a typo of "rides"). So c1 is fine.

c2 "repairs 25%" as a declarative with verb repairs and complement 25% — no subject. Grammatically possible as an elliptical clause ("repairs 25%" = "[it] repairs 25%"), but the natural reading is a label "repairs" with value 25%.

Is this a wrong statement? "repairs" as a verb states an action; the message lists categories. Per the settled case pattern for label/value lists (like n=116 and n=120: "add a cat 260 Take 2" where "Take" was made a verb), hmm.

C2 and c3 have no subject and their "verbs" are nouns (repairs, spares). I'd say L1: "Its `verb` is a word that is no verb here" — "repairs" here is the name of a slice (like "spares"). Hmm, but "grammar allows a word as noun or verb" is a pass criterion ("A word that grammar allows as a noun or as a verb: 'make y axis scale linear'"). Hmm! That criterion exists to protect exactly this kind of ambiguity.

Hmm. Then, is a coordination joining c4 (fragment "one pie chart") with c1, c2, c3 fine? And the nouns-as-verbs pass.

Ugh. The pass rule "A word that grammar allows as a noun or as a verb" — "repairs" in "repairs 25%" — as a verb phrase "repairs 25%" needs a subject; in a coordination with "the wedges rides 30%", the subject could be shared: "the wedges rides 30%, repairs 25%, spares 45%" — subject sharing? Not written for c2/c3 though (they have no subject). Hmm.

OK: for n=116, the reading "the wedges rides 30%, repairs 25%, spares 45%" with c2/c3 as declaratives lacking subjects → the labels are verbs. I think this is a rejection: the three labels "wedges", "repairs", "spares" are slice names each with a percentage; making "repairs" and "spares" verbs loses the labels as items and states actions. But the pass rule about noun/verb ambiguity...

Let me compare with n=120 "add a cat 260 Take 2": "Take" as a verb of an imperative clause with complements "260" and "2" — "Take" is capitalised (a name?). Hmm.

I'll decide: for n=116, accept? Hmm. Think about what's lost: the pairing "repairs 25%" is preserved (verb repairs, complement 25%). The word "repairs" is there. The next layer sees "repairs" as a verb and can reinterpret. Nothing is lost except the label reading. Hmm, it's a plausible reading.

But the "form" declarative for "repairs 25%" — a fragment-ish part written as a declarative clause states something the message doesn't say (that something repairs 25%). Hmm.

Given the explicit pass rule for noun/verb words, I'll accept n=116 as L8. Hmm... but "the wedges rides 30%" — c1 fine.

Hmm, honestly, I think the reference judge likely rejects this one, since "repairs 25%" and "spares 45%" as declarative clauses is a stretch with no subject. But the rules' pass list protects noun-or-verb words. I'll accept — being lenient per the instructions ("reject only a wrong statement or lost explicit information").

Hmm, wait. L4? "a `subject` the words do not show" — c1 has subject "the wedges"; c2/c3 have no subject written (they don't claim a subject either, so no L4). OK accept.

n=117: "Could you what values does Lunch orders show?. Thanks!"
c1 interrogative verb "Could" subject you (no verb after Could!); n2 "what values"; c2 interrogative auxiliary does verb show subject n3 (Lunch orders); c3 fragment discourse Thanks; k1 coordination c1, c2.

Hmm: c1 "Could" as the VERB of an interrogative clause with subject "you" — "Could" is an auxiliary; L1: "Its `verb` is a word that is no verb here, or an auxiliary while the main verb stands elsewhere." Here "Could" is an auxiliary and the main verb "show" stands elsewhere (in c2). So L1!

Yes: "Could" held as the verb while "show" is the main verb → L1. Quote 'Could you what values'.

Hmm, but the message is garbled ("Could you what values does Lunch orders show?" — two templates). Still, "Could" as verb = auxiliary as verb with the main verb elsewhere → L1. Good.

Note the settled case: "Could you move it?" is one interrogative clause: "Could" is an auxiliary. Here "Could" is written as verb → L1.

n=118: "please to insert a picture of the old culvert and move it to the right corner"
c1 fragment discourse please; r1 "to" c1→k1; c2 nonfinite insert complement n1; n1 a picture; r2 "of" n1→n2; k1 coordination "and" c2, c3; c3 nonfinite move complement n3 (it); r3 "to" c3→n4.

Hmm. "please to insert ..." — "to insert" infinitive; "and move it" — the second verb is finite-imperative "move" (a command). The circuit makes both nonfinite clauses coordinated under the "to" relation from a fragment clause "please". Per the settled case ("the 'to' of an infinitive is the marker of the relation that ends at the nonfinite clause; when nothing stands before it, the relation starts at the main clause").

Is "move" as nonfinite wrong? "insert ... and move it to the right corner" — "move" is coordinated with "insert", sharing "to" — so nonfinite is fine ("to insert ... and [to] move it"). OK.

So the structure: c1 fragment "please" with the relation to the coordination of two nonfinite clauses. Plausible. Accept L8? Hmm, "please to insert" is odd but the formalizer handled it.

Accept L8.

n=119: "set the bend of arrow from Start to Review to 26 and the x to 120 and the y to 80"
c1 imperative set complement n1 (the bend); r1 "of" n1→n2 (arrow); r2 "from" n1→n3 (Start); r3 "to" n3→n4 (Review); r4 "to" ambiguous c1→n5 (26); k1 coordination with 2 ands: conjuncts c1, c2; n6 the x; r5 "to" n6→n7 (120); n8 the y; r6 "to" n8→n9 (80); c2 fragment complement k2 (n6, n8) ellipsis=c1.

Hmm: "from Start to Review" — r2 "from" from n1 (the bend) to Start; r3 "to" from Start to Review. Reads "the bend of arrow from Start to Review". OK-ish.

Accept L8.

n=120: "add a cat 260 Take 2"
c1 imperative add complement n1 (a cat); n2 "260"; c2 imperative verb "Take" complement n2 (260), complement n3 (2); k1 coordination c1, c2.

Hmm: "add a cat 260 Take 2" — garbled. "Take" as a verb in an imperative clause with complements "260" and "2". n2 "260" is held as a complement of c2 (Take) rather than tied to "cat". Hmm.

Is this wrong? "add a cat 260 Take 2" — likely "add a cat 260" + "Take 2"?? Honestly garbled ("Take 2" = a retake marker). The circuit holds "260" with "Take" — and k1 coordinates the two imperative clauses.

Per the number-after-noun rule, "260" could be a dependent of "cat" or a nominal tied to it. Here it's a complement of c2 "Take". Hmm, that's a merge: "260" is separated from "cat".

Is there a wrong statement? "Take 260 2" — reading: c2 "Take" takes complements 260 and 2, and the coordination with "add a cat 260"? Hmm, c2's complement includes n2 "260" which is the cat's number. Hmm.

Hmm, "Take" as a verb of an imperative clause: plausible ("Take 2"). "260" tied to it: hmm.

Is a rejection warranted? The number "260" right after "cat" is now in the next clause, which means "add a cat" loses its number and "Take" gets it. Per the case: "A number or a name right after a noun ('block 2', 'x 120', 'the node Intro') may be a dependent in that noun's nominal, or a nominal of its own tied to the noun by a relation without a marker. Both pass. Left tied to nothing, it is L6." Here the number is tied to "Take" — a wrong end? The relation r? there's no relation; n2 is a complement of c2. Hmm — "A nominal is the complement of the wrong clause" (L3)? "260" is the complement of "Take" instead of belonging to "cat".

Hmm, but is "260" the cat's number? "add a cat 260 Take 2" — could be "add a cat 260" (a cat at 260) then "Take 2" as a name. Yeah, plausible.

Grade: L3 ("A nominal is the complement of the wrong clause"). I'd reject. Hmm. Or maybe accept as garbled.

Let me think about how wrong it is: the message's words: add a cat 260 Take 2. The circuit reads: imperative "add a cat" + imperative "Take 260 2". The "Take 2" is a separate item and "260" belongs with the cat. So c2's complement "260" is wrong. But is "260" the cat's? Ambiguous — "260" after "cat" per the case belongs to the cat.

Given the case explicitly says a number right after a noun belongs to that noun's group, taking it into the next clause is a wrong tie. L3. Hmm, but the pass rule "either may be a dependent in that noun's nominal or a nominal of its own tied to the noun" — both require tying to THE NOUN. Here it's tied to another clause's verb → fails.

I'll reject n=120 as L3: "'260' stands right after 'cat' but is held as a complement of the clause of 'Take'".

Now 121-150.

n=121: "draw the diagram, then check the profit area is above zero"
c1 imperative draw complement the diagram; k1 coordination "then" c1, c2 (imperative check); c2 imperative check (no complement); c3 declarative is subject the profit area; r1 "above" c3→zero; r2 c2→c3.

Good. "check the profit area is above zero" — c3 tied to c2. Accept L8.

n=122: "would you make that one look nicer"
c1 interrogative would make subject you (no complement); n2 "that one"; c2 nonfinite look modifier nicer subject n2; r1 c1→c2.

Good: "make that one look nicer" — c2 nonfinite "look" with subject "that one", tied to c1. Accept L8.

n=123: "slide block 15 under block 2, then slide block 15 left to block 14"
c1 imperative slide complement n1 (block); n2 "15" tied; r1 "under" n1→n3 (block); n4 "2" tied; k1 coordination "then" c1, c3; n5 = "slide block" (dep slide(!), head block); n6 15; c2 nonfinite verb "left"(!); r2 "to" n5→n7 (block); n8 "14"; c3 fragment complement n5 ellipsis=c1; r5 n5→c2; r6 n5→n6; r7 n7→n8.

Problem: the second "slide" is held as a DEPENDENT of "block" (n5 deps slide, head block), so the second imperative "slide block 15 left to block 14" is written as a fragment with ellipsis=c1. Hmm — is that OK? The second sentence's verb "slide" is repeated in the message: "then slide block 15 left to block 14". The circuit holds "slide" as a dependent of "block" and makes c3 a fragment with ellipsis=c1 (sharing the first "slide")! That's a wrong statement: the word "slide" is not a dependent of "block"; it's the verb of the second clause. Since the fragment's ellipsis covers it, the second "slide" word is redundant/misplaced → L3 (words in the wrong wire) — the word "slide" (second instance) is held as a dependent of "block" rather than as the clause's verb.

Also c2 nonfinite "left" as verb — "left" is a direction word, held as the verb of a nonfinite clause?! "slide block 15 left to block 14" — "left" should be a modifier. Making "left" the verb of a nonfinite clause → L1 ("Its `verb` is a word that is no verb here").

Hmm, two flaws. Grade L1 comes first? "left" as verb is L1. Hmm, but which to name? Both are wrong statements. I'll write one note naming the clearer: "'slide' is held as a dependent of 'block' and 'left' as the verb of a nonfinite clause, so the second command has no verb of its own".

Grade: L1 (verb "left" is no verb here; and the second "slide" is not a verb anywhere). Good.

n=124: like n=109. Accept L8.

n=125: "the olive treatment for the shape, and olive lettered inside"
n1 "the olive treatment"; r1 "for" n1→n2 (the shape); k1 coordination "and" n1, n3 ("olive lettered": dep olive, head lettered); c1 fragment modifier "inside" complement k1.

Hmm: "olive lettered inside" — "lettered" as a nominal head with "olive" as a dependent; "inside" as a modifier of the clause. Calling "lettered" a head nominal — "lettered" is a participle; per the case, a participle that describes is the verb of a nonfinite clause tied to the thing. Held as a nominal head... hmm. Is this a wrong statement? "olive lettered inside" — the label lettered in olive, inside. As a nominal "olive lettered" with head "lettered" — hmm, "lettered" as a noun? Weird.

Hmm, is it L3 (head wrong)? Or acceptable garbled? The message is a fragment: "the olive treatment for the shape, and olive lettered inside". Both parts are fragments describing styling. Holding "lettered" as a head with "olive" dependent — the next layer reads "olive lettered" as a thing. Hmm, "olive lettered" is not a thing.

I'm not confident. Let me consider accepting: all words placed, tied; plausible for a fragment. Accept L8? The participle-as-head is a bit off but the rules' pass list has "a word that grammar allows as a noun or as a verb" — "lettered" as a noun? no.

Hmm. Risk either way. Considering leniency instructions, accept L8.

Hmm, but hmm: "inside" as a modifier of the clause — fine.

Accept.

n=126: "I walked the team through Revenue trend this morning; nobody argued with the data, only with how it reads at a glance, so as a first pass how about line thinner? and then let's have the marker borders thicker on the revenue trend, then we revisit next week, also put the y axis on the right"
Circuit: c1 declarative walked subject I complements n2 (the team), n4 (this morning); r1 "through" c1→n3; c2 = declarative **interrogative** verb "argued" modifier only, modifier how, subject nobody; r2 "with" c2→n6; r3 "with" c2→c3 ("how it reads"); c3 declarative reads subject it modifier how — wait, c3 has modifier "how"; c2 also has modifier "how"?! Text has "how" twice ("with how it reads" and "how about line thinner"). Yes two "how"s. OK.
r4 "at" c3→n8; k1 coordination "so","and" conjuncts c1, c2, c4, c7, c8; r5 "as" c2→n9 (a first pass); r6 "about" c2→n10 ("line" with dep "thinner"!); c4 imperative let complement n11 ("'s"); c5 nonfinite have; n12 "the marker"; c6 declarative verb "borders" modifier thicker subject n12!!; r7 "on" c6→n13; c7 declarative revisit subject we complement next week; c8 imperative put complement the y axis; r8 "on" c8→the right; r9 c4→c5; r10 c5→c6.

Problems:
1. c2 "nobody argued with the data, only with how it reads at a glance" — written **interrogative** → wrong form (a declarative written as interrogative) → L1.
2. n10 "line thinner" — "thinner" as a dependent of "line" → L3 per the settled case.
3. c6: "the marker borders thicker" — "borders" as the VERB of a declarative clause with subject "the marker" → L1/L3 wrong.
4. r6 "about" from c2 to n10 — the "how about" belongs to c2 (nobody argued)? Since c2 is `interrogative`... hmm.

Multiple flaws. Grade: L1 (c2's form interrogative for a declarative; and "borders" as a verb). Note will quote 'nobody argued with the data'.

Quote: 'nobody argued with the data' — in the message: "nobody argued with the data" — yes.

So n=126 → L1.

n=127: "and also Sales by month: grid line style dash-dot"
c1 fragment discourse "and" complement n1 ("also Sales": dep also, head Sales); r1 "by" n1→n2 (month); n3 "grid line style dash-dot" (deps grid, line, style, head dash-dot); r2 n1→n3.

Hmm, "also" as a dependent of "Sales" — "a word of order"? "also" is an additive adverb. Held as a dependent of the nominal → part of the description? Hmm, L3? "A word of time or order cannot describe a noun" — "also" isn't time/order exactly, but it's like "too" ("the shed walls too" case is in the list!). The case: "A word of time or order cannot describe a noun from where it stands ('orders by week first', 'beside the sun next', 'the shed walls too', 'now a second wooden boat')". "also" is similar to "too" — an additive adverb that cannot describe a noun. Held as a dependent → L3.

Hmm, "and also Sales by month" — the "also" scope is the whole item. Holding it inside the nominal "also Sales" makes it describe Sales. Hmm, "also" before a noun... "also Sales" — hmm, in some contexts "also" can modify a noun phrase ("also John came" — it's a focusing adverb that can adjoin NPs). Hmm, "also" as a dependent of the nominal: "the also Sales"? Ehh.

I'd lean L3 per the "too" case analogy. Hmm, but "also" is not exactly order/time. The case list mentions "the shed walls too" — "too" as a dependent of "walls" fails. "also" is the same family (additive adverb). So L3.

Hmm, risky. Alternatively accept. Let me note "n3: 'grid line style dash-dot' as one nominal with head 'dash-dot'" — that's a merged nominal of property+value, similar to other chains; acceptable-ish.

I'll reject n=127 as L3 quoting 'also Sales' with the note that 'also' is held as a dependent of 'Sales' though it modifies the whole item like 'too'.

Hmm, is that solid? "also" is the second word of the message ("and also Sales by month"), so it's a clause-level word. Held as a dependent of "Sales" — yes, this changes the item into "also Sales". I'm fairly comfortable: L3.

n=128: "This year and last side by side: order value by delivery time"
n1 "This year"; k1 coordination "and" n1, n2 ("last"); n3 "side"; r1 "by" n3→n4 (side); n5 "order value"; r2 "by" n5→n6 (delivery time); c1 fragment complements k1, n3, n5.

"side by side" as two nominals tied by "by" — fine (as n=108). Accept L8.

n=129: same family as n=103 with "and then make the font a bit bigger" as c6 imperative discourse "and" — but c6 is NOT in any coordination! k1 coordinates c3 and c4 only. c6 "and then make the font a bit bigger" is a clause with no tie to anything. Hmm — is it L6? "A clause ... is tied to nothing inside its sentence." Hmm, but c6 is a separate sentence ("... before the meeting starts. and then make the font a bit bigger"). Rule L6: "Separate sentences need no tie." So c6 as a separate sentence needs no tie. Fine.

The "and" at the start of the later sentence held as discourse in c6 — allowed by the case.

Accept L8.

n=130: "Revenue by month of the order date, top five regions only"
n1 Revenue; r1 "by" n1→n2 (month); r2 "of" n2→n3 (the order date); c1 imperative verb "top" modifier only complement n4 ("five regions"); c2 fragment complement n1; r3 n1→c1.

Problem: "top five regions only" — "top" is held as the VERB of an imperative clause! "top" is an adjective here ("top five regions"). L1: "Its `verb` is a word that is no verb here." Yes → L1.

Quote 'top five regions only' — note: "'top' is held as the verb of an imperative clause though it is the adjective of 'five regions'".

L1.

n=131: "add a star called dog; then put dog below owner."
c1 imperative add complement n1 (a star); n2 = "called dog" (dep called, head dog!); k1 coordination "then" c1, c2; c2 imperative put complement n3 (dog); r1 "below" c2→n4 (owner); r2 n1→n2.

Hmm: "a star called dog" — n2 has "called" as a DEPENDENT of "dog", so "called" is a modifier word inside the nominal. Per the settled case: "A participle that names or describes ('a group called g2', 'a bird facing left') is the `verb` of a nonfinite clause tied to the thing. Written as the `marker` of a relation between the thing and its name, it also passes."

Here "called" is neither: it's a dependent of the name "dog". Is that a wrong statement? Hmm. The case allows verb of a nonfinite clause, or marker. "Held as a dependent of the name" — not among the passing options. Hmm, but the rule is about participle handling; holding "called" as a dependent of "dog" makes "called dog" a name phrase — "a star called dog". Hmm, the next layer reads: star, with n2 "called dog" tied. The info is preserved. Is there a wrong statement? Not clearly.

The case says those two ways "pass"; it doesn't say other ways fail. Rejecting needs a quote + wrong statement. "called" as a dependent — hmm, the nominal "called dog" with head "dog" means the name is "called dog" — it's like a multi-word name, allowed ("A name of several words may stand whole in head, or with its last word as head and the others as dependent"). "called dog" could be read as a name of several words! OK accept L8.

n=132: "I showed Budget split round the team; they didn't argue with the numbers but not with how it reads at a glance, so as a first pass make the legend smaller, then we revisit next week; plus show the percentages"
c1 declarative showed subject I complement n2 ("Budget split": dep Budget, head split); r1 "round" n2→n3 (the team); c2 declarative did n't argue subject they; r2 "with" c2→n5; k1 coordination "but" conjunct r2, r3 (relations); r3 negation=not marker "with" from c2 to c3 (how it reads); c3 declarative reads subject it modifier how; r4 "at" c3→n7; r5 "so" c5→c4; r6 "as" c4→n8; c4 imperative make modifier smaller complement n9 (the legend); c5 declarative revisit subject we complement next week; k2 coordination "plus" conjuncts c1, c2, c5, c6; c6 imperative show complement n12.

Hmm: k1 coordinates r2 and r3 (the two "with" relations of c2). The message: "they didn't argue with the numbers but not with how it reads at a glance" — coordinating the two with-phrases. Plausible.

r5 "so" from c5 (revisit) to c4 (make): hmm, "so as a first pass make the legend smaller, then we revisit next week" — the "so" relation starts at c4 (make) typically (the clause after the marker).
